source_label: Conair · 1875 Watt Turbo Dryer Instruction & Styling Guide (285 MODELS, US version)
test_conditions:
Nameplate rated power — the manufacturer prints it directly as watts. The manual’s “GETTING TO KNOW YOUR HAIR DRYER” caption reads, verbatim, “1875 watts” and “3 heat/speed settings”; the supply condition is stated verbatim in the OPERATING INSTRUCTIONS section: “Use on Alternating Current (60 hertz) only. Standard dryers are designed to operate at 110 to 125 volts AC.” Two other manuals from the same brand independently reproduce the same number: the 530 series caption likewise reads “1875 watts”, and the Model 127L features column reads “1875 watts of drying power” — three different product lines, three documents, the same number.

Basis statement (a VA-in-disguise edge case): the manual has a separate section titled “1875 WATT OPERATING GUIDE”, whose body warns that sharing a circuit with other appliances can “trip a 15 amp circuit breaker or blow a 15 amp fuse”; the Model 127L manual states “This appliance was set at the factory to operate at 125 volts”. Together these two statements show that the 1875 rating and the capacity of a 15 A circuit at 125 V are the same number. This site accepts the manufacturer-printed watts figure (see _readme item four: the manufacturer prints W directly, that amperage is a circuit-breaker rating rather than a measured current, and a hair dryer's power factor is close to 1), but it is a nameplate rating, not measured real power, and pages must not claim otherwise.

source_label: Conair · 285 series manual, OPERATING INSTRUCTIONS / SUPER STYLING GUIDE
test_conditions:
A hair dryer draws power continuously at the selected setting for as long as the switch is closed, with no thermostat-style on/off cycling — this is fundamentally different from an aquarium heater (thermostat cuts off at temperature) or a refrigerator (compressor cycling). The manufacturer's manuals describe usage throughout as continuous motion: “Move dryer steadily across each section so that the hot air passes through hair”, “Keep dryer moving as you style”, with no automatic intermittent mechanism; the only automatic cutoff the manuals mention is overheat protection (a thermal breaker) and the leakage protection on the plug, both of which are fault protection, not a working cycle. This field is therefore set to 1.0 because that is how the mechanism works, not as a conservative rounding.

1.0 means only “drawing full power at the selected setting the whole time it is on” — it does not mean the dryer runs for long stretches in a day. Actual use is a few minutes at a time, and no manufacturer publishes a duration, so typical_daily_runtime_h is left empty and daily_wh cannot be calculated.

source_label: ENERGY STAR · Certified Pool Pumps dataset (Hayward TriStar VS 950, SP32950VSP 115V, pd_id 2381304)
test_conditions:
High-speed measurement point, 115 V certification entry. The dataset row reads, verbatim: `model_name` = “TriStar VS 950”, `model_number` = “SP32950VSP (115V)”, `power_w_at_high_speed_measurement_point` = “626.95”, `rpm_at_high_speed_measurement_point` = “2177.34”, `flow_gpm_at_high_speed_measurement_point` = “60.63”, `rated_horsepower_hp` = “1.5”. The stored value of 627 is 626.95 rounded up (under-reporting the threshold by even one watt would loosen the compatibility call by that much).

This is a power reading measured on the calibration curve under the DOE pool pump test procedure — not calculated by multiplying current by voltage. The 13.2 A the manufacturer prints elsewhere is the maximum input current rating, with no conversion relationship to this value; dividing the two yields 47.5, which does not correspond to any utility voltage.

Taking the high-speed measurement point as the point value is an editorial choice; the rationale is recorded in watts_distribution_note: the low-speed point is a load almost any power station can carry, giving it no discriminating power, and the pump always runs at high speed for priming at every startup.

source_label: ENERGY STAR · Certified Pool Pumps dataset (same row, low-speed measurement point)
test_conditions: The low-speed measurement point for the same pump, same certification: `power_w_at_low_speed_measurement_point` = “121.09”, `rpm_at_low_speed_measurement_point` = “1126.02”, `flow_gpm_at_low_speed_measurement_point` = “31.16”, `head_fth20_at_low_speed_measurement_point` = “8.1”. The stored value of 121 is truncated (rounded down at the low end of the range, again the direction that does not loosen the determination). This is the operating condition the variable-speed pump was designed around — the Pentair manual states, verbatim: “setting the pump at the lowest speed for the longest duration is the best strategy to minimize energy consumption.”

source_label: ENERGY STAR · Certified Pool Pumps dataset (same row, high-speed measurement point)
test_conditions: Same source and same measurement point as the running_watts point value (626.95 W @ 2177.34 RPM). Deliberately set equal to the point value rather than left blank: this record's point value intentionally sits at the top of the range, and the range field accurately restates that fact, which is more verifiable than a silent omission. The top of the range is not this pump's physical ceiling — 3450 RPM is, and that speed setting has no published wattage (see absence_verified under startup_surge_multiplier).

source_label: ENERGY STAR · Certified Pool Pumps dataset motor_construction field + Hayward specification page
test_conditions: Three documents point to the same fact, this is not an inference: (1) the ENERGY STAR dataset row has `motor_construction` = “Electronically-commutated Motor”, `motor_design` = “Variable-speed”; (2) the Hayward specification page features column reads, verbatim, “Permanent magnet, totally enclosed fan-cooled motor” and “Upgraded motor drive”; (3) the Pentair IntelliFlo VSF manual describes the drive, verbatim, as “The drive controls the motor's rotational speed by controlling the frequency of the supplied current.” Permanent magnet + electronic commutation + frequency control by a drive is exactly the definition this library uses for the `bldc_inverter` value, putting it in the same class as the mini-split-heat-pump / washing-machine / window-air-conditioner-inverter records. `load_type=inverter_driven_motor` comes from the same source as this field.

source_label: ENERGY STAR · Certified Pool Pumps dataset standby_average_power_w field
test_conditions: The same row's `standby_average_power_w` = “3” (Hayward TriStar VS 950, both the 115 V and 230 V certification entries report 3). The same field for the Pentair SuperFlo VST is 2. The DOE test procedure separately specifies a standby-power measurement for pool pumps, so this is a measured and reported figure, not an estimate. Note that after running the factory default schedule for 14 hours, the pump enters a stopped state rather than losing power (Pentair manual: “the pump will enter a stationary/paused state for the next 10 hours”), so this 3 W is a real daily load.

source_label: Pentair · SuperFlo VS installation and user manual (Table 2: Default Schedule)
test_conditions:
While running at a given speed setting, the pump draws power continuously, with no thermostat-style on/off cycling — this is demonstrated by the manufacturer's own factory schedule: Table 2 gives SPEED 1 = 2 hours @ 3000 RPM, SPEED 2 = 10 hours @ 1400 RPM, SPEED 3 = 2 hours @ 2200 RPM, three continuous run blocks rather than a duty cycle. So taking 1.0 at the speed setting used for the determination is correct — that is how the pump actually behaves, not a conservative rounding.

Note that 1.0 describes “running continuously at a given speed setting”, not “full power for 24 hours a day”: an actual day is 14 hours running plus 10 hours stopped (see typical_daily_runtime_h), and 10 of those 14 hours are at the lowest speed setting. Multiplying 1.0 by running_watts to extrapolate full-day energy use would overstate it by more than double, which is why this library does not provide daily_wh (see energy).

source_label: Pentair · SuperFlo VS manual, Table 2: Default Schedule
test_conditions:
The sum of the three segments in the manufacturer's factory default schedule: SPEED 1, two hours @ 3000 RPM (starting 08:00) + SPEED 2, ten hours @ 1400 RPM + SPEED 3, two hours @ 2200 RPM = 14 hours; the manual then states, verbatim, “After 14 hours of run time and completing its run of SPEED 3, the pump will enter a stationary/paused state for the next 10 hours.”

The low confidence is deliberate: this is one manufacturer's factory default for one pump model, not an industry-typical value and not measured user behavior — actual run time depends on pool volume, water temperature, sun exposure, and local water-quality requirements, and the manufacturer itself notes on the same page that it should be adjusted for pool conditions. Any page citing it must make clear that this is a “factory default”, not “typical.”

source_label: Copeland · Application Engineering Bulletin AE4-1331 R9 (September 2024), page 16, Single Phase Starting Characteristics
test_conditions:
Manufacturer's formal engineering bulletin, verbatim (p.16): “The starting Locked Rotor Amperage (LRA), also referred to as inrush current, is normally six or more times higher than the rated running amperage of the compressor and lasts from 100 to 300 milliseconds until the rotor starts turning.” — that is, the 100–300 ms is the time before the rotor starts turning, not the time for the compressor to reach rated speed.
The bulletin's scope is stated on its cover: ZP16–ZP44K3E and ZP14–ZP61K5E, R-410A, 1.5–5 hp Copeland scroll compressors — that is a residential central-AC model segment, while this record is a window unit with a rotary compressor (this library's own window-unit compressor source is the Tecumseh RK5512Y-AA3A rotary, about 0.5 hp). The manufacturer makes no equivalent statement for rotary compressors.
The same bulletin's page 23 also gives the test method for nameplate LRA: physically lock the rotor, apply the nameplate's maximum voltage, and take the current reading four seconds after power-on as the nameplate LRA; it also states that a lower line voltage produces a lower measured LRA. This is directly relevant to this record's surge_basis=nameplate_lra — nameplate LRA is a steady-state reading taken four seconds in, while this field's 100–300 ms describes the transient that precedes it; the two are not on the same time scale.
